My dad gave me one good sentence about sex and love when I was five: “Sex is what you do when you are older and you find a friend you want to have children with.” Good sentence. Not exactly the whole curriculum. This guide is everything else my parents never taught me, that I've learned the hard way & would like to pass to my kids.

I’m a straight man, and I’m writing from relationships I’ve had with women, so she and her are going to show up a lot. Most of this has nothing specifically to do with being male or straight. The Primal Attraction section is the exception, because there I’m specifically talking about the man-woman dynamic I’ve actually lived.

# What we mean by “love” ❤️

English isn't a scientific language when it comes to love. This leads to a lot of romantic confusion because we don't have one word for one meaning.

One meaning is selfless love—what contemplative traditions call [agape, metta, loving-kindness, divine love](http://love.u-dont-exist.com/), and so forth. In Buddhist metta practice you sit there wishing, may they be well, may they be safe, may they be happy. It's not about them being yours.

Then we use the same word for romantic love (eros): *I want you.* I want your attention and your body. I want to be special to you, and I want our lives tangled up together. I don’t think there’s anything fake or shameful about this.

A good relationship must have both kinds of love at once. Too often, the trouble is there’s a whole lot of *I want you* and hardly any *I want you to be happy.*

Most people fail this test: what would I want if she herself thought she’d be happier with somebody else? But if they can get past the initial horror, the conflict starts to fall apart. Being wanted is part of what makes me want someone.

But the horror is unavoidable, because I can’t wait until I know I’m wanted before I let her know I want her. If we both do that, nothing gets started. And it doesn’t stop being true once we’re together. If I start feeling less wanted, I may pull back. She feels me pulling back and starts feeling less wanted herself, then she pulls back too.

Agape or divine love does two jobs at once to rescue the erotic love. First, most obviously, it keeps eros from becoming totally selfish and fickle by making the other person's happiness part of the wanting: I want you because I know you'll be happy with me. Second, it gives eros a landing pad. When two people pull away because eros seems unreciprocated for a moment, the backdrop of actual, genuine care, keeps the couple from simply abandoning each other, and then they might even rekindle the eros when they see that it's based on something deeper.

Eros can help build the agape too. It has a drive to it: it keeps pulling me toward this particular person, and over time that closeness can grow an agape that survives the drive itself.

That drive can weaken for reasons that aren't really my fault. I can get old, sick, depressed, or grieving, and I would hope the agape is deep enough that she sticks by me through some of that even if it puts strain on eros. But if I just get bored with life, stop having much of a life outside her, and make her responsible for nearly all my warmth, meaning, reassurance, and excitement, that's different. I don't get to be shocked if she wants me less.

If the eros does fade, maybe the agape is enough to keep us together. But *maybe* cuts both ways. If I tell her, “Even if I stop wanting you, I may still stay because I love you,” what exactly did I reassure her of? I may stay without wanting her. I may leave anyway. If she still wants me, both possibilities are awful.

Some couples may eventually care more about the life they made together than about the eros that started it. Fine. But that isn't the same as one person staying as a concession while the other still wants them. Nobody at the wedding knows which future their bond will become.

# Talk about making love before you do it

From here on, when I say making love, I'm talking about two people who care about each other deeply and feel super connected, using their bodies as part of that connection. If you’ve never experienced this, it may be like trying to explain the taste of an orange. If you don’t know what love is, you don’t know. That’s another conversation, and I'd suggest reading my inner child reparenting guide.

Having sex is just the physical act, whether that connection is there or not. But sometimes it can create the connection also.

That difference is one reason to talk before sex. Most couples wait until they’re already having sex to talk honestly about sex. By then honesty has consequences: it might interrupt the thing that has already begun. The earlier conversation can go places the later one often can’t, and having it is already part of the difference between making love together and merely having sex.

What do you actually desire? What helps your body feel safe? Are there kinks or particular dynamics that matter to you? What has your history taught you about your erotic wiring? What reliably doesn’t work? How often do you each imagine wanting sex, and what would a mismatch mean? Is sex recreation, bonding, sacred practice, stress relief, all of those, or something else entirely?

A lot of people can’t answer cleanly because they don’t know yet. That’s still an answer. *I don’t know, but I’m willing to find out honestly with you* is a much better beginning than silently assuming the bodies will somehow negotiate everything on their own.

Sexual compatibility isn’t just whether two bodies fit. It’s whether two people can stay honest while maximally exposed. If you can talk frankly before your clothes come off, you’ve already practiced some of the trust, attention, and willingness to be seen that making love requires.

Name the possibility of mismatched desire, too. In long relationships, one person usually wants more sex, less sex, or different sex for at least some stretch. It’s one of the great factories of quiet resentment. Talking about how you might handle it before either person is hurt won’t solve it in advance, but it gives you somewhere to begin.

## Can Casual Sex or a Situationship Actually Be Honest?

Your body doesn’t know that you picked someone up at a bar and agreed it was only for fun. Oxytocin, vasopressin, and the rest can start attaching you anyway. Then the next morning, you’re wondering why they didn’t call. Well, not getting pulled in any further is the best outcome still available, actually, since you just played Russian Roulette with a potential life bond to a stranger.

“I don’t know whether I want something serious with you. I’m not pretending I do. I’d still like to have sex.”

Okay. But sex can make a child. If this girl gets pregnant, she’s gonna call you. Then what? You block her? Agree to child support? Try to convince her to abort when she thinks abortion is killing her child? This is what penetrative sex can do. No contraception is perfect.

The STI part is easy: say what you know, or say you don’t know. Feelings aren’t. You can both mean it when you say this is only sex and still have one of you get attached afterward. If you’re both really numb or robotic about sex, maybe not.

Outside a loving poly community or tribe, I think honest casual sex is almost impossible. You have to care what happens to the person afterward. Otherwise you’re using and abusing them for pleasure. Maybe they’re using you too. Congratulations, now it’s mutual.

A lot of “I only want fun” really means, “This is the only version of the relationship that gets me laid.” Sometimes I know I’m hoping it turns into love. Sometimes I only find out I was hoping that when it doesn’t.

And then there’s the situationship, which is hard to define because that’s basically the point. Usually it’s a happenstance relationship based on sex. There’s less communication, and what communication exists is more superficial. Yet it is obviously some kind of relationship even while one or both people refuse to name it. You’re regularly having sex, going out together, spending time alone together, and doing things you wouldn’t do with a regular friend. It feels like it’s filling a relationship void, but only accidentally and occasionally—maybe just enough to keep you from looking for anything deeper.

It can go either way. Often the man wants to keep it undefined while the woman wants commitment, partly because she’s the one risking pregnancy. Whoever keeps it undefined gets the fun without the responsibility. Refusing to name the relationship doesn’t make the responsibility disappear. What they don’t escape is the existential void created by another superficial fix. Doomscrolling entertains you too.

And “Why are you making this heavy?” can be a real question. They may actually mean: don’t you want the fun, and are you about to give it up? My answer would be: I’m trying to understand whether this is really fulfilling me or if it’s drainingly superficial.

I had something sort of like that with H., although ours was much deeper than what people normally mean by situationship. We were BFFs and spent nearly all our time together. She was falling in love with me, and I wasn’t falling in love with her. She felt more like a sister to me, partly because I’m not attracted to white women. Ours wasn’t superficial. It was just painfully uneven.

But here's the funny thing many people don't understand: labels don't actually change anything.

True commitment grows out of relational depth, not a label. If we spend hours telling each other our deepest longings, fears, and problems, I’ll naturally be ready to help when you need me. I don’t need to promise that on paper. If someone says “I love you, I feel you, I’m here for you,” yet they hardly ever talk to you about what matters, that's a red flag.

The person getting more of what they want may think the arrangement is fulfilling. Usually they’re just less aware that it isn’t. In college I had a friend with four girlfriends who boasted about it to girls while trying to get a fifth. I asked him, “But are you really happy?” He said, “No, I’m miserable, dude. I feel empty inside.”

The full conversation is so big that almost nobody would have casual sex if they took it seriously. Which is why almost nobody has the full conversation. I can’t decide what is okay for anybody else. I can say that most people who defend casual sex are not being very honest with themselves about pregnancy, attachment, or what they might owe the person afterward.

If you want something closer to “casual love-making” without quite so many ways to damage each other, you probably need to find a free-love community where the people aren’t disposable, the bonds can be acknowledged, and any children have a village.

# Should you be in a relationship at all?

This is a horrible catch-22. Wounded people get lonely, and loneliness itself can kill. But the wounds that make somebody desperate for a relationship may also make them a terrible person to be in one with. People don’t only trigger each other and learn lessons. Sometimes they terrorize or kill each other.

I’m pretty conservative about this. I would tell most of my friends not to date yet. First love your inner child. If you can’t even do that, forget a relationship for now. Get a cat or a puppy. If you’re dishonest, can’t care what happens to another person, or keep turning every relationship into the same disaster, come on. You’re not ready.

Some people would say that a good relationship can teach you self-love. True. The problem is that you need a good relationship at exactly the time you may be least capable of creating one, recognizing one, or keeping one good. The odds are terrible.

At twenty, I thought I was totally fine until I became enamored with Alba. She was Dominican, and warm in a way I didn’t understand. Kissing your BFF was normal to her. I thought she was in love with me. She did love me and wanted me living with her, but not in the way I wanted. The confusion threw me into a horrible spell for years. I was even a bit suicidal while living with her.

Then Bee cracked me open. My second wife and I were about as in love as two people could be, considering that every other day she would demonize me because of BPD. Before Bee, I didn’t know what In Love meant. Nobody knows until it happens. It’s a completely different kind of reality. It’s spiritual.

Did it heal her? We still can’t understand. During our two years together, it seemed to stabilize and heal some things while provoking her demons even more. Did it heal me? The relationship almost killed me, and I would never undo it. I still love her so much. I haven’t spoken with her in a year, but I love sending her love.

Relationships ALWAYS reveal what I can’t see. My selfishness. The depth that is actually available versus the depth I idealize. The other person’s selfishness and dishonesty and superficiality. How deeply I really love. How deep my illusions go. Whether my spirituality survives contact with another human being. Everything.

I’ve used spirituality as a replacement for intimacy a lot because intimacy was simply unavailable. As a boy and young man, I was so deprived of female touch that it was driving me insane. Meditation sometimes made the deprivation easier. The deprivation stayed.

Most people can’t be happy celibate. Distracted-happy, sure. Truly happy, I don’t believe it. Most people are not so serious about spiritual liberation that giving up sex and partnership for life makes sense. The Buddha didn’t advise most people to become monks.

Maybe you genuinely become happier and more peaceful as a monk or nun. Great. Stay. It might work for some very advanced people, or if your sexual desire is already low, or you’re old, etc.

The hard part is that lack of awareness is an epistemic problem. How do you know what you’re not aware of? Inner-child reparenting can help a lot, because often the inner child is being ignored while the adult is feeling some kind of liberation.

And if you’re so happy and free, what happens when you’re alone in a room with a super beautiful girl and she wants you? Or vice versa for women. Do you feel like you’re losing some control? Are you afraid?

Bhante Gunaratana tells a story like this in his autobiography. A super beautiful girl at a retreat he was teaching snuck into his room and waited for him naked. He went nuts and started screaming at her to get out at the top of his lungs. Obviously he was still repressing something, and she was adept at uncovering it (surely not her intent).

Robes do nothing. I was mildly molested in public by the abbot of one of Thailand’s largest Buddhist retreat centers. In Thailand, parents have very good reasons not to leave children alone with monks. Tibet is worse.

Forced celibacy doesn’t abolish anyone’s sexuality. For most people it eventually sends it somewhere weird. Why wouldn’t it?

And monasticism is not only about liberation. In a poor country, the robe can mean free food and somewhere to live, and you get to escape a lot of ordinary responsibilities. In the West the free food probably matters less. But somebody who got no particular respect as a layman can become Venerable Somebody and suddenly people are bowing to him.

Maybe he sincerely wants liberation too. Sure. Why wouldn’t he? People can want several things at once.

Then there are practical partnerships.

I travel the world as a (white) guy from a first-world country. Many women have wanted to marry me partly because they figured I could improve their status and comfort. That always makes me feel sad and lonely to think about, but yeah, I know it's to be expected.

It’s reasonable for a woman to want support, since after all she has to provide for her potential children, but it muddies the waters for me. I'm not stupid, I understand that she might really love me while still wanting money, stability, children, a visa, a home, etc. Men aren't a different species, although sometimes I think I might be. A man can really love a woman for who she is while also seeing her as a source of sex, children, social legitimacy, or help running the house. Affection and practical motives often coexist, even if it isn't the romantic ideal.

And hey, sometimes being objectified is kinda sexy, too. Men like to be objectified to a certain degree as providers and defenders, just as women often like being seen as sex dolls by the men they want. Being wanted that way feels good, but feeling held is important as well.

I don’t want to be just a provider-and-defender machine, because that's vulnerable to hypergamy. I wanna know that if I fall ill or lose my job, I can count on my wife still. Guys want a ride-or-die chick. A woman also wants to know that when she gets old, sick, or no longer looks like the fantasy that first attracted her man, he will still happily stay.

But beyond all that practical stuff, sex is extremely important for building and renewing the connection. I have also said that if two people aren't having sex, it becomes hard to explain how they're different from regular friends. The apparent contradiction is mostly a matter of timing.

I think sex is especially important while the bond is forming. It may be what turns a friendship into a romance and keeps feeding the romantic connection. But if the connection gets deep enough, sex appeal stops being the basis of the relationship. You don’t stop loving the person because she got old, he lost his job, one of you got sick, or sex became impossible.

Sometimes they may even want you to find sexual satisfaction elsewhere if they can’t give it, because they love you and want you to be happy. Maybe they don’t. Nobody is owed that as proof of love.

Partnership is generally healthier for people who are ready for it. A good community is generally healthier than isolated living. Celibacy may be right for some people. I can’t tell any particular person which life is morally superior.

I would still advise most of my friends not to date yet. They have too many problems. Then again, they are lonely, and loneliness kills. That is the catch-22.

## How to find a partner

Looking for a partner is arguably backward, and can work against you. You can’t help looking if you want one, but once you start seeing every new person as a potential partner, you perform for them and they perform for you. Try to see people for who they are before you think of them that way. Actually it was Bee who kept drilling this into me: "You see a pretty girl, but you don't see the ugly stuff she's dealing with inside."

On the other hand, if you aren't looking for one, then you also aren't filtering & comparing potential matches, which makes you more vulnerable to someone who targets you with their love bombs.

Maybe a good compromise is to look for people that match you without directly looking for a romantic match. Join a local group that fits your interests. Go forage for wild plants, meditate, hike, study philosophy, whatever. At least you have fun, learn something, and maybe make some friends even if nobody attractive shows up.

I would never recommend dating apps based on my own experience, although I suppose it depends on the person. Maybe you don’t care much about spirituality or anything, you’re not unique and don’t care if they are, you just "like big butts and you cannot lie," and they want the same sort of thing. Then maybe the app fits what you're looking for. 😅

Case in point, OKCupid didn't tell me my first wife was going to try to kill me and my family, take my son, and then put me on child support that I can't pay and wouldn't pay on principle if I could. That was the worst choice I ever made.

On the other hand, the app did give me information that I ignored because she was cute and interested in me. Her OKCupid profile almost made her sound like a prostitute, or at least someone who liked casual sex. Both turned out to be true. But once she started chatting with me and I saw the nice photos, I thought maybe she had been joking in the profile or something.

These days almost nobody even has a profile. They just have photos, which is showing you something too.

Ok wait, Judge not, lest ye be judged... An app could be fine as an introduction if you use it as a proper gate. Assume 99.99% of the people there are a bad match for you. If you’re just going to get excited by every cute guy or girl who hits you up, forget it. That’s such an easy way to find a weirdo, a psycho, a mooch, a faker, or whatever. Those people are easy enough to find in modern society in person anyway.

I always tell young guys especially: don’t worry about not finding a girl. Worry about finding the wrong girl. Girls are usually more selective, but they still need to think twice, because they often go for guys who aren’t respectful or mature.

I recently tried Hinge again for a few days while I was in Kenya after my last breakup. I was getting something like a hundred girls interested in my profile every day, so I looked through a lot of profiles. Some were cute but none seemed deep. So the app did tell me something useful.

Sometimes when you don't go looking, others go looking for you! My dad at one point decided I needed a girlfriend. This was long before dating apps, so he suggested we put up posters around the neighborhood advertising me as eligible for girls to date. I was horrified and we dropped the idea. That gives you some idea of the mildly autistic background I’m coming from: we didn’t understand people. That's why it might seem absurd the level to which I'm trying here to help you understand what perhaps is already obvious. 😅

The advantage of meeting through your community, unlike through an app, is that you see someone over time. Other people know them. You see how they act when they aren’t on a date, what they’re like with friends, and what happens when they’re irritated, bored, jealous, or not getting what they want.

Community also supports you regardless of who your baby daddy may be, and you aren’t desperate for just any kind of closeness because hopefully the community already fulfills most of that need.

But if you don't have community, the move is to find someone who is also looking for one that would interest you both. You can visit communities together, or at least make a real plan to eventually live in one together. It’s a wide world, and traveling around looking at possible communities is a supremely good way to get to know someone.

On the other hand, you may end up having sex too fast if you’re traveling together, but I'd still rather have sex with someone who's trying to find a commune with me than someone I met at a party.

# Starting on the right foot

## The window of clarity, and how it closes

For me, the window of objectivity starts closing abruptly once it seems like sex will definitely be happening soon and I’m flowing with that timeline. I begin idealizing her more, and after sex I may suddenly feel unable to leave because maybe she’s pregnant, etc.

Maybe I’m not representative of the modern degen dating scene. If you’re quite numb and used to casual sex, perhaps the window closes later, or even never. But for me, this is the pattern, and it seems like it would be healthy in a healthy, natural, small society.

The attachment theory part isn’t just from my own experience. It comes from reading I’ve done as well. Sex turns on bonding chemistry—oxytocin, dopamine, vasopressin—that usually biases us toward attachment. People call oxytocin the “love hormone,” as if getting more attached should make you feel closer and safer. If closeness was safe when you were little, maybe it does feel a bit like coming home. But if it came with neglect, abuse, or if people disappeared on you, you can get more attached and more freaked out at the same time. You might get anxious or suspicious. You might feel worthless or fight or flight mode may kick in.

Before the wisdom window closes, the main thing is to find out whether you are actually compatible. Do you have the same goals and values, especially around children, health, love, and romance? Where do you want to live? Do you both want to find a community? What kind of relationship do you want with technology and money?

Ask deep questions. Conversation-card games may seem silly, but they can help people get past superficial talk and see if they’re compatible.

But asking, “How do you handle jealousy?” can get me a beautiful answer that tells me almost nothing. I’d rather ask what she thinks she would do in an actual situation. If all she can give me is a general answer, I assume she probably doesn't know yet.

I can learn a lot by talking, but there's a point where more questions mostly teach me what the person says about themself. After that I need ordinary time. Ten profound conversations in one weekend may tell me we can have profound conversations. They don't tell me what she's like on a boring day, or when she's annoyed and doesn't have an answer prepared.

You can also bring the person to a party and see how they act, bring them around your family or friends, or take them to activities you enjoy and see if they really enjoy them too. Try doing what you would normally do in your day alone, but with them, and see how it feels. Is it weird? Are they wondering why you do this stuff? Do they look bored, like they’d rather just hit you up later than be with you while you’re doing ordinary stuff? Can you guys be normal together and not just romantic or dating?

See their negative side first too. If there is no negative side, that’s a red flag for fakery. Ask whether the spiritual story they tell about themselves survives an inconvenient afternoon. How recent is the healing story—two months or two years? Jealousy, abandonment, possessiveness, and the “I’m so much better than I used to be” story may not show up until there is stress and entanglement. By then, of course, you’re stressed and entangled.

Sometimes the only thing I have is a little “wait” feeling. It doesn't prove anything. But if I'm about to ignore a question because I really want this to work, that's enough reason for me to ask the question before I keep going.

If they’re nasty to their friends, family, or other people, assume they will eventually be nasty to you. We mostly seem to get attracted to the inner-child part because we’re coming from our inner child and we want to have fun. But you also need to find out whether there is a healthy adult there before you’re too bonded to want the answer.

## Things get tricky fast

Couples withdraw from friends who aren’t supportive of the romantic dyad, and they also stop telling friends the truth. Friends hear less. Sharp questions start to feel rude. An obvious problem dissolves into, "but I love her," and the small world of the relationship starts feeling more real than the rest of life.

Sometimes withdrawing isn’t wrong. Telling your friend, “Can you believe what my girlfriend is doing to me?” can be a privacy violation. It’s just important to realize what is happening.

The relationship can close off at exactly the point when both people most need a view from outside it.

## Anti-PTSD Can Be Just As Dangerous As PTSD

When I’m in love, I see everything just from the love angle. I should probably admit that before I give anybody more advice.

A friend of mine was talking about PTSD recently, and I said, “I have anti-PTSD.” I coined it as a joke, but even though it feels nice to have Anti-PTSD, it can leave me at more risk than if I had PTSD. Instead of expecting danger, I keep expecting each new woman and each new situation to finally be the beautiful exception. I see the good. I give the benefit of the doubt long after it has stopped being a benefit. Then the false positive resolves into the same old pattern and gives me actual PTSD.

My second marriage to Bee is the clearest example. I knew within a week of her visiting that she saw me as her father. I didn’t know where that might lead, and it seemed like the only avenue to her heart, so I went with it.

That dynamic alone isn’t necessarily the main problem. A lot of women have seen me that way. The question is whether they can hold it lightly, playfully, and curiously, or whether it turns into something deeply traumatic—like they’re acting out a taboo fantasy, or they start taking everything they feel about their dad out on me as if I’m him. With Bee, the main issues were the BPD and that her aunts had badly witchcrafted her as a child. She would tell you the same.

She loved me openly and intensely and seemed to understand me spiritually. Most of all, she said the magic words: “I would rather be with you in the forest than with any other man in a mansion.”

Best drug I ever had.

I don’t know whether it ended up being true. I think it was true in a part of her, and it may also have been the BPD idealization. You have to look at everything from multiple angles. But when you’re in love, you see everything from the love angle. That’s the reality shift I’m talking about. It’s great if the ground underneath is prepared for it. If the rose-colored glasses go on when you’re with the wrong person, they make it even harder to understand what’s real.

So I became the father in a relationship where I wanted an equal. Part of what happened may have been that she eventually grew up, and a daughter who grows up doesn’t want her dad in the same way. That wasn’t the whole story. The two years in between contained enough insanity for several lifetimes. We barely made it through.

Looking back, I’m grateful I loved her. For three months after we broke up, [I trained myself to replace missing her with loving her](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/p/i-ate-loveyhuasca-every-day-for-90), and now, any time I think of her, I feel so much joy and love, which I send her way.

That doesn’t mean I’d advise somebody to knowingly enter a dangerous relationship because it may be worth it. Going in, it helps to recognize your pattern, stop idealizing without becoming suspicious and closed, and have some idea what you’re getting into.

## Beware idealization in either direction

Idealization can be pathological, but it can also come very close to real deep love and appreciation. That’s why it’s so easy to get confused.

So far in my life the main experiences of this have been with Bee and Key. They’re also the two women I’ve actually been in love with, which is probably not a coincidence. Both of them saw me as their knight in shining armor, and that brought out this divine-feminine beauty in them that made me into a real love slave. I’m not Superman out here trying to “save a hoe.” There’s just a natural protector/muse dynamic that sometimes plays out in an exaggerated way.

It shouldn’t have to happen that way, though. It’s a bad shortcut to the divine archetypes.

Legitimately seeing someone as amazing doesn’t depend on what the seeing gives you. Once you start identifying with the way you see them—she’s perfect, this is destiny, I’m the one who finally found her—you’re already lost in the sauce.

The degree of idealization also predicts the degree of demonization for me. I don’t mean this as a clinical diagnosis, but I use it almost diagnostically in my own life. If a woman says, “He’s such a great guy. Of course he has flaws like anyone, but I love him,” that sounds healthy. If she says, “He’s perfect. I can’t find any flaw,” I’m already running.

When the splitting happens, private hatred can replace worship. Then come public accusations, rewriting the whole past and treating every flaw as proof that the person was fake all along. Sometimes the woman who thought I was perfect later accuses me of thinking I’m perfect.

I’ve learned to get nervous when somebody knows too much about me too soon. We’re twin flames. She knows my motives. I’m Lord Krishna. Okay, maybe I really am way better than the other guys she’s found. But if she hasn’t found anything about me that bothers her yet, she hasn’t found all of me.

I still love women I’ve loved before. Sometimes I talk about them because I’m thinking about them. I’m not trying to make her jealous. If she can’t handle that I still love them, she isn’t ready for me.

If she says, “Can you talk less about your exes?” Sure. Maybe I do talk about them too much sometimes. But they still matter to me. If I’m supposed to listen to everything on her mind, I don’t want to have to pretend that isn’t on mine.

I can also idealize a woman by seeing her highest potential and forgetting to look at what is actually there. Maybe I really do see something before she fully lives it. I still need to ask whether she wants to reach for it too:

“I see this in you, and I think it’s special. Do you wanna reach for it together?”

If she says no, forget it. You’re in la la land. If she says yes, ask what is blocking her. Is the block more than you can handle? Or does she mostly need somebody to join her on the journey and believe in her?

Partners should help each other grow. Who else is going to do it? Your mom and dad? You’re already grown. Everybody else will usually be a smaller influence, so you’d better choose someone who helps you grow well. Like the FM Laeti song here says, “Inspire her to see the best in herself, actualize that.” If something severe is happening, sometimes a demand or boundary is necessary too.

So hold your horses a bit more than you’d like to. See if your partner still praises you after a cold feud.

Ask what flaws she sees in you from time to time. Notice whether either of you is relating to a real human being or just to the divine archetypal energy the other person temporarily opened.

I’ve been through the wringer so much with idealization that now no matter who praises me I’m basically like, “Okay, thanks.” I try to do my best.

# Two Pillars Don't Hold The Roof Up

Even if you find your twin flame, she’s still only one person, and that's more of a problem than it seems at first. Polarity does not make two people sufficient for each other. A couple still needs friends and community.

Let me show you how this looked for me. I’ve noticed in my own relationships that whenever a serious issue arises, both of us tend to turn to our separate circles of friends for support. Then I resent the one-sided story she’s telling, she resents the one-sided story I’m telling, and eventually neither of us wants to talk to the other’s friends. Some of the friends may even be exes who want us to break up. By then, the outside support isn’t really shared support anymore.

When you rely on your partner to provide nearly all the friendship, family, therapy, and spiritual meaning, the burden is overwhelming. That's too many hats to wear even for a hat model. Besides all that, there's no security when two people have to cover all the life essentials: housing, money, children, emotional, health, and other crises. Who even has time for the relationship itself at that point?

Romantic love can last, but it needs the right conditions, and community is one of them. Both people have to support it, and support from a community makes that much more realistic.

Community isn’t magic either. A very strong couple without much trauma can often do well without community, although it’s a struggle and I think it’s rare. A weak couple might not work even with a community if both people are too weak individually. It depends on the couple.

But having more people around the relationship changes what the two people have to carry. Mutual friends can notice patterns neither person sees. Somebody else can comfort your partner when you have become the wrong person to do it. And when people actually know both of you, they have some chance of telling when the story they’re hearing does not match the person they know.

That's not abstract to me: I'm sure B. and I would still be together if we'd had a real community around us. Most of all, she would not have been capable of demonizing me when everyone already knew both of us and knew I wasn’t a narcissistic abuser. It would have contained all the insanity. Baseless accusations only work with friends who only know one side.

Commune friends could also have helped her in ways I couldn’t, because she was projecting onto me, which made me the wrong person to help her see beyond the projection. And it's actually natural to be a bit BPD when your entire survival depends on one person, because if they aren't perfect, and especially if you need a lot of support, how will you survive? One fairly normal but large flaw in them could make your life really difficult. We were left alone inside something that needed other people around it, and that's what's happening to most people these days.

H. taught me another part of the same dyad problem. I learned not to treat what either of us thought the relationship was as a guarantee of what it would remain, because feelings can and usually do change over time. In our case, the relationship continued to naturally deepen while our outside relationships often felt more shallow, so it was natural for the dependency to increase. She was never into monogamy, but that didn't stop her from becoming possessive once she found something really worth keeping. And then she began demonizing me when I refused to be possessed. Because we did not have a shared community capable of supporting us, her friends heard her side and affirmed her truth. The accusations couldn't have survived among people who knew us both.

Separate confidants can be helpful and harmful. Sometimes you need privacy from your partner and somewhere else to say what you’re feeling. But if your confidant doesn’t have a good connection with your partner, the conversation can turn into an echo chamber very easily.

Having the same confidant creates the opposite problem: now you may not have a release valve when you want privacy from your partner. There isn’t one perfect arrangement.

If you do have separate confidants, you need enough emotional maturity to remember they will automatically be biased toward you. Take what they say with a grain of salt. They are hearing a partial story, usually while you’re upset, and they may be trying to protect you rather than understand the relationship fairly.

So if you don't have a real community already, what can you do about it practically, right now?

Make as much community as you can wherever you are. Go to meetups together. Make deep friendships together. Find some shared purpose beyond maintaining the relationship. Introduce your old friends to your partner and try to mutualize those friendships as much as possible, so they aren’t experienced as slyly antagonistic or partial to one side. You don’t need to spend all your time together, but two completely separate social worlds will automatically start taking sides when something goes wrong.

I do think romantic love can last for a lifetime. I just don't think two people should have to become each other's entire social world to keep it alive. So keep your friendships. They aren't automatically a threat to the relationship; they're part of what keeps you healthy enough to be in one.

# What are you actually choosing together?

A lot of romantic pain starts with two lovey bunnies entering one of the biggest arrangements of their lives without ever discussing their ideas, dreams, and fears about it.

“We’re together” ... what does that mean exactly? It conjures up for me thoughts of romance, sex, exclusivity, living together, shared money, children, caregiving, spiritual partnership, family identity, or just “we really like each other and we’ll see.” Lack of specificity is sometimes a nice way to flow, but the problem is that each person could be imagining a different bundle from those pieces, then either not labeling anything or assuming one relationship label settled it.

One honest option is basically a "practical partnership." This is very common, especially outside the modern West. Two people may share a home, raise children, support each other financially, take care of each other, and maybe have sex, without pretending the whole thing rests on overwhelming romantic love.

Although this feels wrong to me and anyone else who has been in love, arguably, there is nothing inherently wrong with that if both people know that’s what they are doing. This arrangement has been promoted throughout history because it isn't based on highly fluctuating feelings, but ironically, that's also what can make it unstable. Imagine you're in this, and then one day you find your heartthrob at work or church or somewhere else, and suddenly you wonder why you ever settled for less.

Another honest option is a romance with humility, even if romance and humility seem to clash. Two people really are in love, really do want to build something together, and really do take the bond seriously, but they do not pretend they can guarantee the feeling forever.

They can still choose exclusivity, shack up, have children, and plan a life. The honest part is that they admit feelings can change, and they talk beforehand about what that would mean. If the romance fades, maybe they revive it, or maybe they renegotiate the arrangement.

My actual ideal is to have intimacy embedded in community.

Obviously most people are not going to live in a free-love community unless we really have a New Earth soon. But, as Pema Chodron says to prisoners when teaching them meditation, "Start Where You Are." Build mutual friendships, and keep other sources of meaning and support alive.

Before you commit to one type of relationship, ask each other some real questions:

What are we deciding to join together, and why?

Is this mainly a romance, a practical partnership, or both?

Are we promising actions, or quietly pretending to promise permanent feelings?

If the romance changes, which parts of this agreement still remain?

And the biggie: what happens if one of us falls in love with someone else?

What counts as betrayal, and what just means we need a serious conversation?

Which needs should still be supported mostly outside the relationship?

How should we plan on revisiting this agreement when our lives change?

If we separate, what do we still owe each other, and what do we owe any children involved?

These are just a few questions I could think of to start the ball rolling, but be creative and see what you come up with! You can make a card game out of this and have some fun with it. If there's real love, it will survive a bit of honest curiosity.

## Why marriage vows are dishonest

Conventional marriage vows are dishonest, and most people know it. You can't promise how you'll feel in the future. You can promise actions if you really believe you're capable of delivering them. So for example, you could promise to tell the truth, to keep showing up, to support the children, or whatever else you genuinely believe you can do.

We also find something like my warning in the New & Old Testaments. Ecclesiastes 5:4–6 explicitly states that it is better not to make a vow than to make one and not fulfill it, warning that God will be angry with your words and destroy your work if you say to the priest, "I didn’t mean what I promised." It's also interesting that promising itself is almost an indicator of dishonesty: Matthew 5:33–37 (and parallel James 5:12) teaches that believers should let their "Yes" be "Yes" and their "No" be "No," warning that anything beyond this comes from evil.

Where did the idea of promising to have romantic interest in your partner come from, anyway? It turns out it never existed in any culture I'm aware of until the Victorian age, when romantic feelings were elevated in England to the status of immutable truth.

You can sign a contract about what you’ll do. You can’t sign one saying what your heart will feel ten years from now and expect the contract to produce the feeling.

Marriage itself is a sham in many ways. You could honestly say, “I’ll love you to the best of my ability, in accordance with how you love me.” But “I’ll always love you more than anyone else”—based on what? Because God wants you to?

### Attraction and exclusivity

Sexual exclusivity has a different history. Strict sexual exclusivity backed by law and social enforcement grew alongside agriculture, settled property, and inheritance, and became a mass norm during the Industrial Revolution. Tribal cultures across the world have generally had more flexible forms of primary partnership, or 'social monogamy,' with accepted ways for sexual or emotional connection to exist outside it.

Those origins still matter. Property and inheritance are still built into marriage, even while modern vows ask the same institution to guarantee a permanent romantic feeling.

I haven't done any of this perfectly. At one point I tried a more radical answer: changing attraction itself. B. wanted to marry me, but I was still attracted to other women. I told her, “It’s not fair of me to commit to you if I’m still attracted to other women, so before I do, let me see if I can fix that.”

I meditated for a while and surprised my own self to find something like a switch in my mind. It felt like evolutionary programming around whether I had found my life mate and true love. I asked myself, “Is she the one?”

The inner Magic 8 Ball came back YES, and I flipped off the mate-finding switch.

It worked about 99% of the time. I was no longer interested in other women, aside from one extremely beautiful girl who grabbed my attention once. That amazed me, although B. never quite believed the switch was real. She even started hallucinating that I was looking at or talking to other women when I wasn’t. So her jealousy was not simply tracking what I was doing in the present. More likely it was insecure attachment from childhood trying to justify its continued existence.

Jealousy is always insecurity, but sometimes that insecurity can be an important indicator that the relationship actually is not secure, rather than just a remembered script from childhood. Although, either way, it can become a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Instead of stewing in jealousy and throwing out microaggressions now and then, say the actual thing without hiding the insecurity behind anger. In a monogamous relationship, you might say:

“I notice you pay attention to this other girl more than me, and it makes me feel unloved and insecure. Can we talk about it? Do you really want to explore things with her? If so that's fine, but don't make the decision lightly because it's irreversible.”

In a polyamorous relationship the boundaries might be more negotiable, but that actually means negotiating is required.

Maybe he really is neglecting you or wanting to be with someone else. Maybe the “attention” was one glance and your baseline insecurity inflated it into a threat that it wasn't. That part should not be projected onto your partner. Every couple has to work out for themselves what actually feels healthy.

I do believe two people can choose sexual exclusivity honestly. They can admit that attraction to other people exists and decide not to act on it each day.

I would rather make every attraction possible to mention casually, including the low-stakes ones. If only the serious attractions are supposed to be disclosed, each disclosure becomes such a major event that people are less likely to say anything at all.

That's not to say that polyamory is automatically better, because it can be dishonest too. These days, I believe it is often a way to cope with an inability to connect deeply with one person, or a way to admit a lack of self-control without necessarily doing the self-development that would make the arrangement ethical. If you can't do monogamy, saying so is still more honest than pretending you can. Sometimes the pretending does more damage than an outside connection would have.

A foundational, permanent, exclusive romantic partnership is promised far more often than it is actually lived.

# Doing it consciously 🧭

I learned most of this by screwing it up. Some of it I just thought through, and I’m still not sure about all of it. All of this advice is also way too idealistic and unrealistic, and I expect most people will fail at most of it, as I have. But even if they can implement a portion, it will help.

The next two tools reach in different directions. Imagination lets us examine futures we haven't lived. Psychedelics can sometimes get past defenses hiding what is already here. Either one can also give idealization better scenery.

## Imagination as a discernment tool

I'm sure I'm not alone here. Everyone does this. You meet someone and you automatically start imagining how good it could be to have them as your partner. You start thinking you know this person because of how your fantasies went, but really all you know from that is what you want. Actually, that's the most useful thing about the fantasy, to figure out what you want. But I usually make the mistake of playing out just the first part of the fantasy.

I think imagination can work a lot better for starting relationships right if we use it against our tendency to idealize people. So for example, I might start with the regular lovey sexy stuff, and that's fine because that's what's drawing me in. Then after that, when I have a bit of wisdom available, I will continue onto the mundane and difficult scenes. I'm not trying to force anything or oppose anything. I just try to open my eyes when they want to close, ignore, look away. Here's my checklist:

- What's it feel like after we have sex? Do we feel comfortable and happy about that, or do we feel guilty that we gave in to temptation too quickly and now there's some weird feelings? Name the feelings and explore.
- How about a week into the relationship? What's starting to get annoying perhaps? What are we trying not to say and not to notice?
- Get in the ring before the ring gets on you. Let's imagine we have a real fight about money, jealousy, or something else important. What do we do to handle the conflict?
- Fast forward. Now we've got kids. What might be the values conflicts in how we raise them? Schools, screen time, vaxes, religion, helicoptering vs freedom, food, gender & sexual orientation issues.
- Rewind. What if we disagree on having kids?
- Fast forward five years. What has each of us gained or given up, and do we have any resentment about it?

This isn't to make predictions and we're not consulting the magic 8 ball nor doing Istikhara here. I mean you can do that too if you want. Distinguish between fears and what really seems likely just as you do between wishes and reality.

If every scene is beautiful, consider that you may be, and almost certainly are, still rehearsing the relationship you want. There's nothing wrong with expecting the best, but it takes work to get there in a wise way.

Psychedelics can make this same problem of idealization much stronger.

## Psychedelics in relationship discernment

This section will be relevant to some readers and easy for others to skip.

Psychedelics, especially certain types of shrooms, very pure LSD, very pure therapeutic-grade MDMA, ayahuasca, [loveyhuasca haoma](http://soma.u-dont-exist.com/), and [iboga](http://iboga.u-dont-exist.com/), can be extremely useful when a couple is trapped in defensive stories.

With Bee and Key, there were many times when we could argue forever sober, then take something and finally understand each other. It could feel like we were telepathically synced. Instead of each person defending their version, we directly understood what the other was perceiving, feeling, misunderstanding.

But the problem is most people are lazy about integrating what they learn during this window of clarity. We enjoyed the understanding while it lasted, and then the same defensive story would resurface later. In neuroscience, this is called state-dependent learning. What you learn in altered states doesn't automatically translate into your normal sober mind state without the work to do that.

Starting a relationship through psychedelics has another danger. Key and I met and then spent a few days taking iboga with friends. We got to know each other very deeply that way, and that was great. But it was especially her higher self I was getting to know. I tend to idealize people even sober, and that gets worse when I'm high. It was still beautiful to see the real higher self potential in her, I'm not denying that. But that information didn't help me understand how we would get along in normal life.

I’ve also had friends get together at MDMA parties and stuff. It’s rarely a good idea. The intimacy can be completely real. You may feel that this person understands you more deeply than anyone ever has. There is still a lot you don’t know: what happens when you’re sober, irritated, jealous, broke, bored, or trying to make a difficult decision together? Or you might even sometimes have the opposite problem, like I had with H.D., where the connection continues to deepen while sober, and it becomes something that one person might cling to desperately, never imagining they could find that again.

The obvious advice is to wait before making large promises and spend time together sober, around other people, and in ordinary situations. Write down what each of you learned, do some peer counseling, check with friends to see if you're too pie-in-the-sky. But the problem is, you won't necessarily be interested in sober advice when you're high. You're "beyond all that." And the high can continue after sobriety because intimacy itself is like rose-colored glasses.

The main takeaway here is, don’t let the medicine become the only time when you can understand each other, forgive, or remember why you’re together.

# If you’re already in it

One person can’t create mutual honesty. I learned that in all three of my reference relationships. Actually, it’s probably just common sense. I could keep bringing up the same problem, but I couldn’t make the other person look at it with me.

With Bee and Key, the biggest thing sitting underneath everything was trust. They wanted to be with me and would say they trusted me, but really they didn’t trust me, themself, or anyone else. It was all or nothing: blind trust, or none.

I kept saying, “It’s not possible to have a relationship without trust.” I think that rigidity came from trauma and never really growing up.

Even dishonesty was sometimes hard for me to define in these relationships. Bee once opened a door and, a second later, said she hadn’t opened it. That drove me crazy. Why would she lie like that? But looking back on it now, I could have just seen it as some kind of mental illness rather than "lying" since there was no strategy behind it, and in fact she was usually quite honest.

Some things were less mysterious. They were acting as if the trust problem wasn’t there because they still wanted the relationship. Attractions to other people sometimes went unsaid too, and sometimes got imagined from nowhere. Some people keep a relationship like this going for a long time, just sweeping everything under the rug.

I'm not saying to start dumping every hidden thought on your partner and announcing that you’re finally being honest. Ask whether both of you actually want to prioritize radical honesty, first.

Once you've agreed honesty is important, start with the pinkest elephant in the room:

“I don’t think we really trust each other.”

“I’m resentful about this.”

“I’m attracted to somebody else.”

“I don’t know whether I still want the same kind of relationship.”

See whether the other person will stay in the conversation. If they won’t, that tells you something another perfectly worded speech probably won’t fix.

Usually one person wants to open this door before the other. If I'm the one asking for honesty, I have to be willing to hear that the relationship may need to change in a way I don't want. That's where the selfless kind of love from the beginning comes in. But the other person can't keep saying “not now” forever. After a while, refusing to choose is a choice.

## Outside help can sometimes break the loop fast

Bee and I were once desperately misunderstanding each other, so we called my friend Eshwar, the only friend of mine whom she respected. He told a related story about something that had happened with his sister. Somehow, Bee immediately understood what I had been trying to say. It was like magic.

So, don't think of outside help as a formal last resort. I think of it as a part of building community when we learn to rely on each other for this kind of intimate, real-life support. It could be calling up a mutual friend, peer counselor, couples therapist, doing Imago dialogue, Restorative Circle, and/or joining a men’s or women’s group. The key is that both people need to respect the person or process enough to hear something new.

Outside help has a limit: “The only one you can change is yourself” is partly true. Restart whatever you stopped doing because the relationship was soothing you: inner-child reparenting, meditation, body practices, peer counseling.

## What will honesty produce?

Many people ask this question of honesty, but it's unfair. Honesty doesn't produce a certain outcome. It is its own reward.

It might repair the relationship, open it, turn the romance into friendship, preserve the family through separation, or show you that ending it is better.

Temporary separation helped Bee and me. It also became more permanent, although I’ve always thought maybe we would get back together in a few decades.

If the other person won’t look, you can’t make it mutual. Then you have to decide what you can live with.

# Children

I think everyone generally agrees that parents have more responsibility to children than they do to each other, since children can't take care of themselves.

Before having or adopting children, sit down for an imagination session to figure out whether you two lovebirds can preserve some civil co-parenting capacity after a terrible breakup. That's the actual long-term commitment.

When it comes to stepchildren, even if they aren't technically your children, they still become attached. If you've been acting as their parent for years, it's not right to vanish from their life just because the marriage ended. You don't have parental rights legally, but you can stay a mentor or close friend, and hopefully your partner would agree with this. When children have parental figures come and go, it can damage their ability to have good relationships as adults.

Never recruit children into the adult war. They get their own relationship with the other parent.

Children are already involved even when you think you're keeping them out of it, so talk to them directly and honestly. Don’t make them the mediators. It depends on their age, obviously, but you can say something like: “I’m sorry that you see Mommy and Daddy arguing. Sometimes in life even people who love each other can’t understand each other well. We’re trying our best to understand each other, and we’re always hoping we can do better. You’re not responsible for this, and we both love you very much. Hopefully you will be better at understanding your partner in the future.”

That is the ordinary case. My situation with my first wife, Ann, became an extreme exception with two separate decisions. If the adult war is so bad that the child is unavoidably in the middle, sometimes the best thing you can do for the child is to leave the relationship. Stopping contact with the child is a different decision.

This was particularly difficult for me because Ann was very much unfit at the time to care for our son, Bear. I did fight for custody, but, as my lawyer told me, there was no point, because men generally lose. Eventually I exhausted my options for fighting, and I was left with weekly supervised visits.

Ann was brainwashing Bear into believing that I was "breaking his bones" at these visits even though he didn't know what bones were. That's when I told him I had to stop the visits before I end up in jail. So it was for my protection, but his as well, because if he realizes one day his dad is in jail because his mom manipulated him into telling a dangerous story, that could really wreck him.

As it is now, he may miss me, but he is well cared for (I think) by his grandmother, and probably soon he'll seek me out when he gets his own phone.

It takes a village. The nuclear family, built on parents' romance, can often be the worst arrangement for children. If there's trouble in paradise, parents will try to protect the kids by hiding their tension. But the truth is, children absorb that unresolved tension and integrate it into their very being. In a community, romance is one bond among several, and adult stability for children doesn't rise and fall with it.

# Ending consciously

[NATIVE YOUTUBE — preserve from Substack source — videoId: SitT9ojqV1U]

Whether to leave and how to leave are separate questions.

If leaving feels right, then just go. You don’t owe it to them to try counseling unless you also owe it to yourself. If you actually don’t want a good relationship with them anymore, go. No amount of counseling will fix something that has nothing at the base of it.

If you love them and wish it could work, ask if they feel the same, and then go to counseling. On the other hand, even when you love each other, sometimes you already know the issue is beyond what counseling could fix.

Do you have irreconcilable memories of key events? I did with both my first and second wives. I took my first wife, A., to two counselors. A very good one eventually told us, “I’ve never told anyone this, but you guys need to split up for at least six months.”

There's no way to resolve a situation where one person remembers that you ruined her life on purpose, while you remember that she was having a manic episode and had to be committed for her own safety. We also didn’t have mutual friends who could corroborate what happened—only friends on each side who were partial.

If you’ve been there for someone, don't abandon them in a crisis unless it’s unsafe for you to stay or they're creating the crisis to keep you, or they aren’t willing to help themself. You may need to arrange other care. That doesn’t mean you have to pretend the romance still has a future.

Many say it's best to save face and work things out privately, but I'd disagree. Recruiting friends into the conflict is often exactly what you SHOULD be doing. If you don’t have friends who can help with the conflict, then you’re really stuck (and you might wanna find some new friends). But do it honestly, with the goal of helping the conflict, not just getting approval for your own interpretation. Both people should have a chance to speak, and good friends shouldn’t automatically validate either side.

I can believe a friend's experience and still tell them that my ability to know what is really going on is extremely limited. If someone says, “I don’t have all the evidence,” I trust their thinking more. Living in community would help because your friends would not only hear two stories afterward. Sometimes they would actually see how the two of you treat each other when you argue.

## After leaving

Often times the breakup is hard, but the aftermath is worse. Public demonization should be avoided, but that doesn't mean you should hide the truth about the relationship just to save face. Sometimes the truth is abuse, coercion, or serious deception. How much you say, who you say it to, and how public you make it depends on what happened and why you are telling people.

Part of that truth-telling is that a breakup can also expose things you genuinely couldn't see while you were bonded. Seeing them now doesn’t automatically mean you are demonizing the other person. Try to see the situation from their perspective. Try to see where they may be internally conflicted. Don’t jump straight to the conclusion that they were fake all along merely because that story makes the whole relationship easier to explain. Don’t rule it out either if it is actually the most parsimonious explanation.

Seek opinions from people who aren’t heavily invested in seeing your innocence. A therapist, a pastor, or even a stranger can sometimes look at the evidence more clearly than a lifelong friend, and even the curiosity itself can be therapeutic for you.

Spiritual practice during an ending is critical, but it shouldn't be about bypassing your feelings. Pray for your ex's wellbeing. Remember what was real and good, and refuse to use your pain as permission to hate them. Avoid the New Age belief that everyone is simply a mirror of you. No, that isn’t true. We partly mirror one another, but each person is also their own unique person, forged from their own influences apart from you. No matter how enlightened the Buddha was, Devadatta still kept trying to kill him. Looking honestly at your part doesn't erase theirs. Sometimes it helps to ask, "What would Mr. Rogers do?" (if you're old enough to remember that show).

I also learned that public demonization doesn’t always have to be the last chapter. If you avoid contact forever, they might never apologize and learn. Doormat mode would be letting them back into your life without making them lose face themselves through a public apology. Allowing an apology is not the same decision as resuming the relationship.

Going back to someone who's already gone through that cycle can be foolish. But realizing they need to apologize publicly for demonizing their ex can really help some people develop honesty.

## What I gained from loss

At this point, I can say I'm better off because of what happened with B., K., and H., without pretending every part of those relationships was beneficial or destined. Loss taught me things love alone never would. And as Rumi said, "You must keep breaking your heart until it stays open."

From B., I learned what it means for me to be really in love. I learned the kind of woman I actually want: deeply spiritual, sensitive, creative, unique, somebody who inspires me and makes me question everything.

K. repeated a lot of that, which is why I fell in love with her. I learned some of the same harsh lessons from both of them: don’t take openness and curiosity to be fully good. They can also indicate that someone hasn’t developed their own sense of self or opinions, or enough inner adult.

From H., I learned that I can be extremely close to someone and feel completely understood and supported without actually falling in love. I still treasure the support we gave each other.

Too many people judge a relationship only by the result, so start measuring what you actually learned from it instead. Relationships are a process of growth in many dimensions. The result is not only whether you stayed together.

# Tough Love

Romantic love ain't easy, but it is priceless, and the things that actually make it work are not very marketable. I can't sell you the fix with one click or one monthly subscription to my love class. (Just kidding, click here!) It's worth every penny if you ask me, but I can’t give you a formula that makes it stay, aside from the obvious 1+1=2.

Making it work takes both people. That's rare, and probably why romantic love has been seen with suspicion as a destabilizing force throughout history.

One of the best books that makes that point today might be the one I was reading with K: The Spirit of Intimacy, by Sobonfu Somé. Somé is coming from the Dagara tribe in Burkina Faso. To her people, marriage is an arranged, ritualized spiritual and communal responsibility. They're suspicious of romance. But one of her ideas fits what I’m trying to say: when two people come together, something appears between them that is larger than either person alone. She calls it the spirit of the relationship.

I don’t think that spirit belongs to us. Nobody can command it to remain. At our best, we serve it. We tell the truth, keep doing our own inner play & work (pl/ork), ask the community for help, and listen for what the relationship is becoming. When we start thinking we own it or deserve it, that presumptuousness tends to push it away.

My parents agreed with Somé that community matters and that we serve Spirit. They were also not romantic, though they were loving and poly. I actually wished they were in love with each other, I guess, although I couldn't have articulated that since I didn't even have that concept at the time. Also reminiscent of Somé, they also wore rose-colored glasses and taught me that everybody was basically good. So I learned something about love and community, but not how hard romance is without a community around it, or how much damage basically good people can do when their fears, trauma, and undeveloped parts take over.

It took me many decades to figure out what probably everyone else already knows: real private pathology exists. But pathology is also like mold: it festers when the environment is perfect for it. The dominant culture seals two people together, calls that privacy, tells them one person should become lover, family, community, therapist, and future, and then treats the damage as a purely private failure.

The myths around romantic love become real because we co-create them. We act as though jealousy proves love, permanent feelings can be promised, conflict should stay hidden, and the relationship failed if it ended. Then we suffer inside ideas that were never natural laws, and we walk blindly into our first, second, third, fourth, and fifth marriages!

Speaking of which, I wish I’d prioritized understanding the basic fears, desires, traumas, values, strengths, and weaknesses of the women I got close to in a more conscious manner. Instead, I often went with the flow of conversation and hanging out until closeness had built itself before we had decided what it meant.

On the other hand, with H., maybe we had the opposite problem. We reached real depth quickly. That depth kept pulling us toward romantic partnership even though, instinctually, we felt more like family. Depth is powerful, but you still have to ask what kind of relationship you’re actually building.

Maybe this whole article is the rest of the sentence my dad gave me when I was five. And maybe I wrote it for my son, Bear, who sadly, I last saw when he was about five.

Bear, sex can be what you do when you’re older and find a friend you want to have children with. But learn who she is before closeness makes the decision for you. Let her learn who you are. Keep friends around who know both of you. Don’t ask one woman to become your whole village. Don’t imagine they love you when they want you, and understand the difference between possession and commitment. If the relationship is real, treat it as something sacred without pretending you own the outcome.

That’s what I wish my dad had added. That’s what I’m trying to give you here.

## Desire is expressed differently for men & women

Women often make their wanting obvious. They ask, reach, name what they want, and ask a man to do things for them even when they could do those things themselves.

A man's wanting often comes out as doing: providing, fixing, heavy labor, trying to become indispensable. It isn't that he needs less. Part of his need is to be needed. Women also tend to say their emotional needs more directly. That lets them get supported more often and by a wider social net. Men, on the other hand, tend to keep their needs to themselves or put them all onto their woman, especially the need for a confidant.

If a man is too "needy," it tends to turn women off. The way women see it, a man should be in control of himself and able to satisfy his own basic needs. After all, how is he supposed to provide for somebody else if he can't manage himself?

It's not that male pursuit is a turn-off to women (assuming they are interested in the man), but they want to see that the man can pursue strongly while staying grounded. The polarity evaporates when he keeps reaching without satisfaction, loses control of himself, or makes the woman responsible for regulating his emotions.

# What are you actually choosing together?

A lot of romantic pain starts with two lovey bunnies entering one of the biggest arrangements of their lives without ever discussing their ideas, dreams, and fears about it.

“We’re together” ... what does that mean exactly? It conjures up for me thoughts of romance, sex, exclusivity, living together, shared money, children, caregiving, spiritual partnership, family identity, or just “we really like each other and we’ll see.” Lack of specificity is sometimes a nice way to flow, but the problem is that each person could be imagining a different bundle from those pieces, then either not labeling anything or assuming one relationship label settled it.

One honest option is basically a “practical partnership.” This is very common, especially outside the modern West. Two people may share a home, raise children, support each other financially, take care of each other, and maybe have sex, without pretending the whole thing rests on overwhelming romantic love.

This feels wrong to me and to anyone else who has been in love. Arguably, there is still nothing inherently wrong with it if both people know what they are doing. Societies have promoted arrangements like this throughout history because they don't rely on highly fluctuating feelings. The practical side can be stable for exactly that reason. What may be unstable is the romance somebody gave up. Then one person meets a heartthrob at work or church and suddenly wonders why they settled for less.

That isn't the option I want. I want romance. The honest version has to admit that it cannot guarantee its own feeling forever. Two people can really be in love, really want to build something together, and really take the bond seriously without pretending they know the future. That's romance with humility, even if the two words seem to clash.

They can still choose exclusivity, shack up, have children, and plan a life. They admit feelings can change and talk beforehand about what that would mean. If the romance fades, maybe they revive it, or maybe they renegotiate the arrangement.

## Why marriage vows are dishonest

Conventional marriage vows are dishonest, and most people know it. You can't promise how you'll feel in the future. You can promise actions if you really believe you're capable of delivering them. So for example, you could promise to tell the truth, to keep showing up, to support the children, or whatever else you genuinely believe you can do.

Ecclesiastes 5:4–6 says it is better not to make a vow than to make one and fail to fulfill it. It also warns that God will be angry with your words and destroy your work if you tell the priest, “I didn’t mean what I promised.” Matthew 5:33–37, echoed in James 5:12, says let your “Yes” be “Yes” and your “No” be “No,” and says anything beyond that comes from evil. Those passages are not talking about romance. But they make me suspicious of the promise itself: if my plain yes isn't trustworthy, why would more swearing make it so?

Where did the idea of promising to have romantic interest in your partner come from, anyway? It turns out it never existed in any culture I'm aware of until the Victorian age, when romantic feelings were elevated in England to the status of immutable truth.

You can sign a contract about what you’ll do. You can’t sign one saying what your heart will feel ten years from now and expect the contract to produce the feeling.

Marriage itself is a sham in many ways. You could honestly say, “I’ll love you to the best of my ability, in accordance with how you love me.” But “I’ll always love you more than anyone else”—based on what? Because God wants you to?

### Attraction and exclusivity

Sexual exclusivity has a different history. Strict sexual exclusivity backed by law and social enforcement grew alongside agriculture, settled property, and inheritance. It became a mass norm during the Industrial Revolution.

Tribal cultures across the world have generally had more flexible forms of primary partnership, or “social monogamy,” with accepted ways for sexual or emotional connection to exist outside it.

Those origins still matter. Property and inheritance are still built into marriage, even while modern vows ask the same institution to guarantee a permanent romantic feeling.
